subject: Reasoning
description: Strong vs weak arguments, relevance judgements

questions.stem: Statement: 'Should the government ban the use of all single-use plastics immediately?' Argument I: Yes, single-use plastics are a major source of pollution and harm marine life. Argument II: No, such a ban will disrupt small businesses and cause job loss. Which of the following is correct?
questions.explanation: A 'strong' argument is relevant to the statement AND backed by a verifiable consequence. Argument I cites a documented environmental harm (valid and relevant). Argument II cites a real economic consequence (also relevant; small plastic vendors, packaging MSMEs). Both touch the actual policy trade-off, so both are strong. A ban IS a policy question that weighs environment vs livelihood — both sides need serious weight.

questions.stem: Statement: 'Should India introduce a four-day work week for all government offices?' Argument I: Yes, this will reduce traffic congestion in cities. Argument II: Yes, a global famous tech CEO has endorsed it. Which argument is stronger?
questions.explanation: Argument I cites a measurable public-interest consequence of the policy (lower congestion is testable and relevant). Argument II is a classic 'appeal to authority' — a famous person endorsing something is not itself a reason for a policy to apply to India's context. Authority alone is a WEAK argument in this exam framework.

questions.stem: Statement: 'Should school education up to Class 10 be made completely free for all children in the country?' Argument I: No, parents who can afford it should pay. Argument II: Yes, because the Right to Education is a constitutional mandate under Article 21A.
questions.explanation: Argument II is grounded in an enforceable constitutional principle (RTE under Art 21A, + the RTE Act 2009 mandates free education in neighbourhood schools for 6-14 age). That is strong. Argument I is a bare preference — it doesn't engage with the rights claim, and doesn't address whether means-tested subsidies would work; it is weak as stated. Constitutional-mandate arguments are usually stronger than consumer-preference ones in this framework.

questions.stem: Statement: 'Should cigarettes be banned in India?' Argument I: Yes, smoking causes lung cancer, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease and many other illnesses. Argument II: No, because smoking is a part of our traditional culture.
questions.explanation: Argument I cites well-established medical consequences — relevant and strong. Argument II rests on a factually questionable and weak 'tradition' appeal — mass cigarette smoking in India is a 20th-century commercial phenomenon, not a long-standing cultural tradition, and even traditions do not always trump public-health harm. Appeals to tradition are usually weak when they clash with verifiable harm.

questions.stem: Statement: 'Should mobile phones be allowed in examination halls?' Argument I: No, they will be used for cheating. Argument II: Yes, mobile phones are used everywhere in modern life.
questions.explanation: Argument I is directly relevant to the purpose of an examination (fair assessment) and cites a specific, real risk. Argument II is a generic appeal to ubiquity — 'because it exists elsewhere' — and does not address the specific integrity concern of an exam. Weak.

questions.stem: Statement: 'Should students be awarded marks based on class participation?' Argument I: Yes, it will encourage active engagement and reduce rote learning. Argument II: No, shy and introverted students will be unfairly penalised.
questions.explanation: Both arguments engage with the real trade-off of the proposal. I cites a pedagogical benefit (engagement over rote). II identifies a concrete fairness cost (inhibition of introverted learners). Both are specific, relevant and backed by reasonable consequences — classic 'both strong' case in this format.

questions.stem: Statement: 'Should interest rates on home loans be reduced?' Argument I: No, because banks will lose profits. Argument II: Yes, lower rates will boost the housing sector and related jobs.
questions.explanation: Argument II addresses a broader public-interest effect — housing demand, construction jobs, multiplier impact — classic macroeconomic logic. Argument I captures only one specific stakeholder's profit interest, not the policy's overall merit; weak because it ignores whether higher volumes could offset thinner margins. Public-policy arguments need to weigh broader consequences, not just one group's narrow loss.
